# Work

> Work is a free, open-source desktop app for getting work done with AI agents: your projects, a real browser, terminals and editors, and agents that reshape the app and build tools for you. It runs on your Mac, uses the AI accounts you already pay for, and keeps your work on your machine unless you choose to run your own server.

> Canonical copy: https://work.software/llms.txt (this file mirrors it with repository-relative links; keep both in step, see docs in the website repository).

Work is the product; Catamorphic is the open-source framework it is built on. Both live in one repository: https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic (Apache-2.0).

## Facts

- Product: Work, "the software for work"
- Framework underneath: Catamorphic (same repository)
- Framework libraries: public `@catamorphic/*` npm packages, released at the same version as Work; Preview installs use `@alpha`, Stable uses `latest`
- License: Apache-2.0
- Price: free; no account, subscription or hosted service required
- Platform: macOS 13 or newer on Apple silicon (desktop); a mobile web companion; the Work server, a library composed into your own deployment
- Releases: Preview only so far. Every release is a pre-release, and Stable has not been published yet.
- Install: `brew install --cask opencx-labs/tap/work@alpha`, or the DMG on https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases
- AI: your own Claude Code or Codex account, your own Hermes Agent, or API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter); providers bill you directly
- Data: stays on your Mac by default; optionally on a server you run
- Work server: install a pinned `@catamorphic/work-server` release, compose a small TypeScript entry point and hooks, and build your own image; Work publishes libraries rather than a stock server image. PGlite needs no external service; network Postgres supports disposable replicas. One deployment serves one trusted organization or household.
- Connect other tools: MCP (your server is an MCP endpoint: your own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, starts a coding agent on it, keeps working, waits for it, answers its questions and reads its result and pull requests; each project is an endpoint too, with its documents and workflows), and an HTTP API with an OpenAPI description and a generated TypeScript client
- Website: https://work.software
- This guide, with the linked documents inlined: https://work.software/llms-full.txt
- Source of truth for capabilities: the repository's README and decision records (links below)

## What matters most

- **Open source and free, no strings attached.** Apache-2.0 license. No account, no subscription, no hosted service required. Nothing leaves your machine unless you send it.
- **It is a browser.** Work embeds a real Chromium browser: tabs, profiles, bookmarks, history, a password manager with passkeys, and Chrome extensions from the Chrome Web Store. Agents drive it as you would, in your signed-in tabs. You can use it as a clean browser and nothing more.
- **It uses your existing AI subscriptions.** Sign in with the Claude Code or Codex account you already have, or add API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter). Providers charge you directly; Work adds nothing.
- **Completely local, or your own server.** The desktop app runs with an embedded database and local sandboxes; no cloud. When you want your work and agents available from your phone or while the Mac sleeps, run the Work server yourself (your own deployment built on `@catamorphic/work-server`) and keep everything on hardware you control. A company brain on that server can admit only its Google Workspace accounts, revokes a departed person's access within minutes, lets agents reach company systems without handing them credentials, and shares specific documents, folders, or apps with customers behind their own sign-in.
- **Easy to get started.** A Tutorial tab walks through themes, AI agent setup, the dock, keyboard shortcuts, palette modes, sidebars and browser setup, and can be opened again from the palette.
- **Completely customizable.** The sidebars, the chips above every chat, command palette modes, theme, shortcuts, tabs, notifications and terminal macros are plain files. Ask the assistant to change them and it edits the files; the app updates live. Agents build apps and workflows inside a project that look and behave like built-in parts of the app.
- **Three ways to use it.** A coding workspace (worktrees, terminals, editors, diffs, pull requests, several coding harnesses side by side). A company brain (shared projects, roles and memberships, automations, apps, tuned agent roles, reachable from desktop, mobile PWA or any MCP client). Or just a nice, clean browser with an assistant a keystroke away.

## Why it exists

We built Work because we believe one well-built piece of software can replace most productivity and collaboration tools. Software is now cheap; as humans, we just need to find the optimal form for it, make it open source, and let it build itself afterwards.

## How it works

### The desktop app

- New profiles open in Default Project with the dock collapsed on the right. The default right sidebar contains only the agent customization button.
- The Tutorial opens as a normal tab, with themes, AI agent setup, the dock, keyboard shortcuts, palette modes, sidebars, and combined browser setup. Done opens a normal New Tab palette. Search for onboarding or tutorial in the palette to revisit it. Choose theme opens the same live theme picker from the palette, Settings, or onboarding.
- Chats float over whatever you are doing (a page, a document, a terminal) and can be minimized to a dock, which can also float in a window of its own. Each turn, agents see the workspace context in front of you: the page, the file, the terminal.
- Work restores every workspace window after Quit or an update restart, with its profile, grouped projects, tabs and layout, placement and last focus. A restart for an update never waits on running agents: they continue once Work reopens.
- The command palette can rename the current chat or close the current Work window. Its History mode finds the current project's chats by words in their titles and user and assistant messages, with a matching excerpt, and combines these with the profile's opened pages and work by recency. Tool output and reasoning are not searched.
- In a message, "/" lists the chat's commands and skills, and "@" mentions open tabs, files, chats, workflows and apps.
- On macOS, Finder's Open With menu and Work's Dock icon accept PDFs, images, media, web pages, text and code without changing the default app. Text and code open in the current project's editor, or as plain text in a browser tab when no project is open. Other supported files open in a browser tab. Reopening an editor file reuses its tab; browser files follow the Switch to a page's open tab preference.
- For code: worktrees, terminals with shell integration, diff tabs, and pull request review with per-file diffs. Claude Code loads a repository's CLAUDE.md and its `.claude` skills, agents, commands and settings as its CLI does.
- Voice:
  - Hold a microphone or shortcut to talk with your assistant or any chat, then release to send. Pauses never send a message.
  - macOS uses Apple's native speech recognition: SpeechAnalyzer on supported macOS 26 devices, SFSpeechRecognizer otherwise. Apple's older recognizer may use Apple's servers when on-device recognition is unavailable. Work does not install speech-to-text or speaker-detection models on macOS. The Linux build, not yet released, uses local Parakeet.
  - Reply voices use local Kokoro, and any agent reply can be read aloud from its button. Pressing again interrupts playback.
  - Dictation inserts your words on release wherever your cursor is: in Work, a web page, or, on macOS once allowed in Accessibility, any app.
  - The microphone and macOS audio lowering stop on release while buffered transcription and replies finish.
  - Voice keeps what was on screen as you pressed, with screen access once allowed.

### The browser

- Tabs, Chrome-style profiles, bookmarks (pinned tiles and lists, per project too) and history. Tabs can sit in the sidebar instead of the top bar.
- Work can be the system's default browser. Bookmarks, history, passwords and, where the other browser allows it, signed-in sessions import from another browser's profile.
- Passwords: Work offers to save sign-ins, suggests saved logins under the field, generates strong passwords for new accounts, and keeps notes with each login, unlocked with Touch ID.
- Passkeys: sites can create them, and you sign in with Touch ID from a sheet or the field suggestions. Security keys work alongside. Passkeys and passwords import from Bitwarden or KeePassXC (passwords from a CSV file too).
- Sites that use Chrome's built-in Translator and LanguageDetector work as in Chrome, on the device: Firefox's translator, its model for a language pair downloaded the first time a page asks, and Google's CLD3 detector, so page text never leaves the computer.
- Tabs you have not looked at for a while sleep to free memory and reopen where you left off, as in Chrome.
- Any tab, a chat or terminal too, can be pinned: it stays first in the strip as its icon, Cmd+W and closing all tabs leave it, and it comes back after a restart.
- Incognito tabs keep no history and run no extensions, and their cookies and sign-ins go when the last one closes.
- Chrome extensions install from the Chrome Web Store with Chrome's permission prompts and verified packages, with pinned toolbar buttons and popups, side panels, keyboard shortcuts and an Extensions page: uBlock Origin Lite and Dark Reader work, and the Claude and ChatGPT extensions drive Work's tabs as they drive Chrome's.
- Each site has one place for its permissions (camera, microphone, location, notifications and others: ask, allow or block) and its stored data. Downloads save without a dialog, show progress on the dock and are listed on a Downloads page. A page that asks to share your screen can be given any tab of the window, with sound as a choice.
- Agents drive the browser as you would, in your signed-in tabs: real clicks and typing, uploads and downloads, and a page's console, network and JavaScript for web development.

### Customizing Work

- On macOS, choose your own running Dock icon in Settings > Appearance, or reset to Work's default; the choice applies to all profiles.
- The sidebars, the chips above every chat and command palette modes live in `workspace.js`, the theme in `theme.json`, and shortcuts, tabs, notifications and terminal macros in settings files. A theme can put a picture behind the sidebars and the chat, and a profile can take another profile's settings once or stay in sync with it.
- Every sidebar list, Work's own tabs, chats and bookmarks included, and every chat's chips are a source the assistant can wrap in a few lines of code to sort, filter or group it, or replace with data from anywhere.
- That code runs confined, on macOS and in the Linux build that is not yet released: it reaches only the lists, addresses and files its package.json declares, and Work asks you before it runs and again whenever it wants more.
- Links and images an agent writes reach only hosts you trust. Work asks before opening a link or showing an image from any other host; you can allow it this once or trust the host from then on, and everyone automatically trusts the project's approved published host list.
- A chat's chips show its tabs, subagents and pull requests (with their live state and checks), and agents attach their own, such as a preview deploy, without code.
- A Resources list, which you can add to a sidebar, shows what Work runs by who it runs for: each chat, terminal, browser tab and sidebar module with its CPU drawn as a live line and its memory. It ends a stray process with one click.
- Customizations use an installed typed SDK, a static checker and previews through the actual confined runtime. Apps and sidebar sources share the same handles for calling and starting workflows and following their runs.
- Member-private workflows, versioned state and notifications use the ordinary workflow engine without requiring a chat or Git repository. Explicitly enabled application services and private schedules continue under a separate background runtime after the desktop UI quits. Private source and data are not uploaded merely by connecting a server.
- Native action forms support choices, custom dates and repeated entries. Inspectors offer readable facts, copy actions, rich prose and sandboxed app content; persistent project lists retain focus and expansion as context changes.

### Projects, agents and chats

- A project is an ordinary folder that can hold documents, notes, data, code, automations and apps in any mix. Work uses Git where the folder is a repository, and a plain folder you open stays plain until an operation needs Git.
- In a project Work created, and in a chat's own worktree, every agent turn that changes files becomes a checkpoint commit; you can inspect diffs or trust routine work to continue. In a folder or repository you opened or imported, Work commits nothing by itself.
- A chat can work in a worktree of its own, set up before its first turn. Archiving the chat puts the worktree away on its branch, and its changes come back to the project folder or are discarded when you choose.
- Agents can be Claude Code, Codex, API models, your own Hermes Agent (added in Settings, with its own model, memory and sign-in), or an Agent Client Protocol agent a project names, which runs its own command on the desktop once you approve it, or in its sandbox on a Work server.
- Each agent has its own sandboxing, skills and instructions. Claude Code and Codex agents also choose a permission mode in the harness's own terms (Claude Code's plan, auto or bypass permissions; Codex's sandbox and approvals), effort is set where the harness takes one, and Claude Code agents can keep memory.
- Connectors (MCP servers, found in the official registry or in plugin marketplaces) attach to profiles and agents, and each of their tools can be set to allow, ask or deny.
- A project can commit its own agent definitions, which appear in every collaborator's picker. A committed definition runs on your personal credentials only after you consent to it.
- Change a chat's agent at any time between turns, including between Claude and ChatGPT. The same conversation stays open; each harness resumes its own native thread with a bounded summary of the turns it missed and access to full session history.
- Subagents:
  - Agents start copies of themselves, or other agents they are allowed, on the model and effort the work needs (a stronger model for a hard design, a quicker one for a broad search) or read-only for a review (in Claude Code and Codex). Agents on a Work server start them too, from their sandbox.
  - A subagent works in its parent's workspace by default: the same files, as they are, with nothing to set up again. Parallel writers ask for one of their own, started where the parent's started. A shared workspace asks only for the connections a subagent requires, so an optional connection the workspace lacks is left out.
  - Each runs as its own chat you can open. Its reports reach the parent's working turn automatically, including a result it reaches in a later turn; routine progress folds into expandable activity with full reports and source links, while failures and requests for your input stay visible.
  - An agent's settings say which agents it may start and which models and efforts it may choose; by default it may start copies of itself on any model and effort.
  - A tool call that waits, such as waiting for subagents, ends before the agent's client would give the call up (after 45 seconds for an Agent Client Protocol agent, by default) and says so, so the agent waits again with the subagents still running.
- Typed results: an agent's definition can declare them (JSON Schemas). The agent submits them with `submit_result`, only a value the schema accepts is recorded, and parents and workflows read them instead of parsing replies. Each is recorded with the chat, turn and input that produced it and the commit of the workspace it was produced on, a shared subagent's included, so a rule over several agents' results can compare commits.
- Chats you run in Claude Code or Codex outside Work can appear among the project's chats (in the palette and any list of them), once you turn it on in that agent's settings: only chats started after that, kept current as the CLI writes, and never synced to a server. Any agent can continue one. An agent on the original harness resumes its native session when available; another harness receives a context handoff.
- Every chat is a durable log of turns, the same on the desktop, the phone and the server, streamed live. Questions and approvals can be answered from any of them.
- A message sent while an agent works reaches it at its next step, and you can have it read at once; one sent while the agent waits on a question reaches it in the same turn.
- A chat can be forked from any message into a new chat.
- When the server process that ran a turn stops, another picks the turn up where its sandbox survived. Where the agent's own process is gone, the turn ends as interrupted and the chat continues on the agent's own conversation in a new turn.
- Undoing a turn undoes every later one too. The files return to where they stood before it in a workspace the chat owns, or in a project folder nothing else changed since.
- Agents run long commands in the background, on the desktop and on the Work server, where they run inside the agent's own workspace and stop when the chat closes. On the desktop agents can also watch a command (a deploy, a file, a status page); the chat wakes when it finishes, succeeds or changes, including after the computer sleeps.

### Workflows, automations and apps

- Agents write durable workflows (TypeScript, run in sandboxes, resumable) and apps (small React screens built from Work's component kit). The code is the source of truth, and Work draws a workflow as a graph people can read. An app can read your own chats in a project after you allow it once; it never sees anyone else's.
- A workflow is made of retry boundaries, pauses with timeouts, child workflows and paged batches with per-item progress. A project's workflows can be served as tools, and its apps as MCP Apps, to the MCP client a person already uses.
- A workflow declares the project permissions and the store documents it uses, and whoever turns it on approves both. Its runs reach only those documents.
- Automations run for you or for the whole project. A workflow starts from a schedule, a chat event, or a webhook sent to your server, and can message your chat or a shared project chat that anyone in the project can continue (one per pull request review, one per inbound request).
- GitHub's webhooks are included. Where no webhook can reach the server, a polling workflow (a ready-made pack) records the same events, so webhook automations run unchanged; on the desktop, a chat's own watchers poll GitHub.
- On a Work server, people joining, leaving, or changing groups in the company directory start workflows too, so a new engineer's keys are issued as they join and revoked as they leave.
- Projects define their own triggers, such as "a pull request was merged" or "someone mentioned the app in Slack", on top of webhooks, with filters that decide which events start a run; webhooks check each sender's signature scheme and answer its setup handshake.
- Chat events cover a chat being created, messages, turns, work being completed, a typed result being recorded, an opened request, a stalled turn, and a workspace being made, moved, given back, lost or set up.
- A workflow acts on chats with the same operations people and agents use (start, send, wait, read, answer, interrupt, close). It can also run commands in a chat's workspace (copying a trusted review procedure into it, or adding a new revision beside its checkout) and get their output back.
- A command that outlives its step (a long install during setup, a long test run) parks the run: the run gives back its own capacity while the command goes on in the chat's workspace. Following a parked command needs no machine placement, so the run resumes with the command's result wherever its work is placed next.
- Hooks are triggers. Where project code should run at a point in Work's own lifecycle, Work records an event and workflows bind it in their own source; no configuration names a workflow. Such an event can be waited for: Work asks which project automations listen, records the event, and waits until every run it started has ended. With no listener, nothing waits. Setting a workspace up and deploying a revision are the two such events today.
- Workflows see when a chat's turn last made progress and what it is running; an agent can set how long a turn may go without progress, Work tells workflows when one does, and a workflow can collect diagnostics, then restart the turn, which keeps the runner's and the agent's own error output with each attempt that did not finish.
- Each attempt of a turn also records how long each part of its preparation took (waiting for a machine, waiting for a workspace another chat is preparing, making or starting the sandbox, checking out the base, restoring the chat's work, each part of setup, starting the agent, and its first output), written as each part starts and ends, so a project's workflows and members read where a chat's time goes, and where a stuck one is, without keeping a ledger of their own.
- When an unattended agent needs approval, the people its automation named get a notification and answer in that chat, or a project workflow answers: every approval, question or prompt an agent's turn waits on is a session event, `session.request-opened`, and a project automation bound to it approves or denies in code. While one listens, an approval in a chat no one watches waits for its answer (two minutes by default where no person approves) instead of being refused at once.
- Project automations follow the published program: merging to the project's main (on its code host, or publishing from Work) deploys them, unless the new revision asks for more access than was approved, which waits for a person and tells them. A person's own automations, which use their own accounts, follow only once they choose to. A workflow that does not build at a revision keeps running the previous one, and a passing outage never makes it skip one.
- Deploys:
  - A project workflow takes part in a deploy by binding `trigger("project.deploy")` in its own source and being turned on as a project automation. No configuration names a workflow: the manifest's `"deploy": { "workflow": ... }` is removed, and a revision whose manifest still has it does not go live and says to bind the trigger.
  - Work records the event once for each try of a published revision, before the automations that follow `main` move to it, and waits for every run it starts to succeed. The event's `detail` carries `commit` and `previousCommit`.
  - The runs execute the workflow as the new revision declares it, under the automation's existing authority, and only when that authority is unchanged there. A listener whose authority the revision changes fails the deploy until its update is approved; a workflow already turned on that starts binding the trigger is one, since what starts it changed.
  - With no listener there is no deploy step. Several listeners all run, and all must succeed.
  - A failure keeps the previous revision live and tells the people who manage the project's automations. The next published revision gets its own deploy; the latest failed one is tried again when someone who manages automations asks, or once by itself when a listening automation is approved again.
  - Work does not know what a deploy workflow does: its own database migrations, or nothing.
- A Work server's hooks can give each new project its own credentials, such as a database URL, kept as project secrets, and clean them up when it is deleted.
- Glue code is normal: workflows compose ordinary TypeScript, npm SDKs, durable boundaries, webhooks, schedules and external Postgres state. Work server hooks supply privileged operations, authorization and callbacks. A missing native integration such as AWS is not a blocker when these primitives express the use case; an external runner need not enroll as a Work worker. Agents should distinguish core defects from application orchestration and prove recovery with the final deployment.
- A workflow boundary and its returned host, document or connection operation share one persisted five-minute attempt deadline. Providers receive cancellation and the deadline, recovered jobs retain the budget, and late results are fenced. Accepted external effects still need application reconciliation.
- Named workflow signals can buffer before their matching pause, scoped to an existing active run id and correlation key. Durable receipts deduplicate callbacks, each signal resumes one pause, and pending values are cleared when the run ends. Signals never follow a restart; callbacks carry the enrollment generation.
- A workflow can make its runs about one subject take turns: `concurrency: { key, onConflict: "queue" }` names the subject from the run's input, and a run whose subject already has a live run waits as `queued`, holding no machine, then starts in arrival order once the runs ahead settle. Workflows read and set a chat's metadata, so state about a chat (a verdict, a posted comment's id) lives on the chat. A delivery (a webhook, a schedule occurrence, an event) starts at most one run of an automation.
- Durable workflow waits give back physical workspace capacity after confirmed teardown. A continuation receives fresh admission with current owner and connection authority and keeps the same deployed revision and journal. Children and batch work share capacity until all their compute waits; workspace files and processes do not survive parking.

### Slack and pull request reviews, built from project code

- Slack is project code rather than a built-in integration: mentioning the app in a Slack thread starts or continues a shared project chat for that thread, the agent reads the thread (and, given a search token, searches Slack) through the gateway, which holds the tokens, and its answer is posted back to the thread. Slack's retries of an event start no second run.
- Pull request review is built the same way. Every pull request of the connected repository that is not a draft gets a code and security review in its own shared chat on a dedicated review pool.
  - The reviewer works on the pull request's head. Setup installs its dependencies; the reviewer builds, runs the tests and the change's services in its own sandbox, checks migrations against a read-only production replica where one is connected, and reports what it found as typed results.
  - A workflow outside the review's sandbox validates the report and posts commit-bound reviews, checks and replies, one publication per pull request at a time. The check shows the review in progress from the moment it is queued (waiting to start, preparing the workspace, reviewing).
  - Findings the reviewer has verified are posted as inline comments while the review runs, up to 30 a turn on lines the diff has; the review's body lists or counts the rest. The review completes the check with its verdict, deciding from GitHub and recording each commit's verdict on the review chat. It comments or requests changes and never approves.
  - The machine running the pull request's code holds no GitHub write access, not even a push.
  - The default reviewer is the built-in agent, which runs on the Work server's control plane, so its model key and Work's tools never enter the review machine. During the review the pull request's own code (its tests and services) reaches only the checkout, its test services and a read-only Git connection. Its install runs earlier, in setup, on a network that reaches only the package registries the Environment lists, with no grant or secret.
  - A project's own Claude Code reviewer runs in a container of its own beside that code, sharing only the checkout, while the open-model OpenCode reviewer, a separate pack, runs beside it unprotected.
  - The reviewer still reads what the pull request wrote, so the review is advice and a person still approves the merge.
  - Each push moves the same chat to the new head. As the pack ships, a push gets a new sandbox and a full install over a read-only package cache that only a fill from main writes; a project workflow bound to the setup event can keep the sandbox and install again only when a lockfile changed.
  - Mentions of the reviewer in comments are answered on the pull request, and merging or closing it releases everything the review held.
  - Every write that creates something on GitHub (a check, a review, a comment, a reply) carries a stamp so a retry finds a write GitHub already accepted, and the recipe leaves descriptions, change-request dismissal and thread resolution to people.
- Reviews, Slack threads and GitHub polling are ready-made packs: an agent installs one into a project when someone asks for it, and the team edits the workflow and agent files in the project; nothing installs into the server.

### The Work server

- The Work server is a company brain composed from libraries and your own hooks. A deployment owns its entry point, dependencies and image, and pins `@catamorphic/work-server`. Anyone can ask their coding agent to set one up with the setup skill.
- Sign-in: built-in local accounts, configured OAuth or OpenID Connect providers, or Google Workspace. With Google Workspace only the company's domains get in, people suspended or removed in the directory are signed out within minutes, and directory groups can map to project roles.
- People join a project through invitation links that carry no credential, and committed role files decide what each member and agent may read and do. A company project keeps its reviewed program (documents, code, workflows, apps, roles) apart from a project store for per-customer and generated documents.
- Agents and workflows reach MCP servers, HTTP APIs and a production database through a gateway that holds the keys.
  - Code running in an agent's sandbox (a dev server, a script, tests) calls HTTP APIs through it with a short-lived session grant instead of a pasted key.
  - Database access is read-only with cost and row limits.
  - A company can add its own guards in code (a model reviewer, a person's approval, or both) to review each action. Work ships none.
  - Organization administrators connect each system once, from the app or the server, and projects choose which of those connections each environment may use in a reviewed project file.
- Project secrets are sealed in an encrypted vault. Projects list the secrets each environment sets as environment variables, with a shared value and a value of each person's own, such as a key issued to every engineer, set by that person, an administrator, or an onboarding workflow; values are write-only and masked in chat transcripts.
- Members can use Claude Code, Codex or another MCP client to read and search the project, draft, check and deploy workflows and apps, run workflows, read results and work with project agents: start one, wait for it in short calls, steer or interrupt it, answer its questions, and read its result and pull requests. The client acts with the member's own roles, narrowed by the scopes the member grants when signing it in; approving an agent's request needs a scope the member grants on purpose.
- People work beside their agents on the Work server: from the desktop, a chat that runs there opens a terminal in its workspace (a login shell with the environment's secrets) and previews a server running there, such as a dev server, in a browser tab by its port. Previews reload by hand; live reload does not reach them.
- A chat started on a person's own computer moves to a server environment and continues there with its history.
- Shares send customers or partners a sign-in link to one document, folder or live app. They sign in with their own account (for example your product's own sign-in over OpenID Connect) and see only what was shared.
- The server exports traces, metrics and logs with OpenTelemetry to wherever the deployment points them.

### Machines on the Work server

- Enrolled workers add capacity. A worker dials out to the server and runs agent sandboxes; workflow runs and every credential stay on the control plane. Each worker holds a machine credential and a key of its own, both rotating, and what the server queues for it is sealed to that key.
- A worker can serve specific users, projects, or chat keys, or anyone whose role and Environment allow it.
- The host's machines hook plans capacity and calls its own infrastructure. Work records intent, retries the same operation, drains safely, and retires lost work so chats can continue from their last save. Without a hook, workers are enrolled by hand.
- Workers can stop and resume with their disk and sign-ins. A stopped machine keeps its images: only the time a machine ran counts toward removing the ones it no longer uses.
- Work that needs a machine waits for one for as long as its Environment allows, and its chat shows when a machine is starting or resuming. The host's plan hears of newly waiting work within seconds.
- A machine unseen for five minutes by default is lost: one the plan still names is made again, and its chats continue on another machine from their last save, without the work done since.
- Work manages disk floors and reservations, removes the images and leftovers it no longer uses, names a full disk in the failures it causes, and sends machine events to the projects the machine serves.
- Copyable registry recipes cover EC2, Hetzner Cloud, running the machine operations through project workflows, machine policy and worker installation. They are copied into the server's own code.

### Sandboxes and Environments

- On the Work server each machine runs sandboxes in the best isolation it has, chosen at start: a microVM where it has hardware virtualization, else a gVisor container on any Linux machine with Docker and gVisor, which the worker installation recipe sets up. A machine with Docker and no gVisor runs plain containers, and one with neither runs plain processes; both isolate less, and operators see each machine's choice.
- Each project Environment chooses:
  - the image its agents run in (a registry image or a Dockerfile reviewed in the project), and the CPU, memory and storage a sandbox gets;
  - whether they get their own Docker and Docker Compose;
  - which hosts they may reach: any, only the gateway, or a list;
  - how a new workspace checks out the project's code: it fetches its commit from the server with Git, whole by default, or by a `checkout` command of the project's own that takes one part of a large monorepo;
  - a setup command every new workspace runs (installing the project's dependencies), which may reach hosts of its own, such as package registries, that the agent's turns do not;
  - directories kept on the machine for each person, such as a package store or a Docker data root, so later workspaces start warm (not together with a setup network of its own).
- A setup command is told what it runs on: `WORK_BASE` (the commit), `WORK_PREVIOUS_BASE` (the commit it last ran on in that sandbox) and `WORK_SETUP_REASON` (`created`, `rebuilt`, `base-moved` or `changed`), so it can install only what changed.
- A project workflow takes part in setup by binding `session.workspace-setup` in its own source. The turn waits for every run the event starts for a project automation, within the Environment's `setup.timeoutMinutes`. Work records the event after the setup command, with the reason, the Environment, the commit the workspace stands on, the commit this sandbox last set up on, and whether the sandbox is `new` or `kept`. A failed or late run is a failed setup: the agent is told and setup is asked again before the next turn. An Environment names no workflow: `setup.workflow` is removed, and a project file that still has it is invalid.
- Setup asks before it replaces a sandbox. With no workflow listening nothing changes: a setup with a network of its own gets a new sandbox and runs in full whenever the base moves. Where a project automation listens and the sandbox already set up, Work replaces nothing and runs nothing by itself, unless another chat's turn is running in the workspace: the checkout moves to the new base in place, what was installed stays, and the event says `kept`. The sandbox is replaced, and the setup command run again, only when a run asks for the setup's network (`exec` with `in: "setup"`). `sessions.changedPaths` tells a workflow which paths differ between two commits of a chat, so a push to a reviewed pull request installs again only when a lockfile changed.
- An Environment can run its agents' commands apart from them: every command the agent's shell, setup, workflows and terminals run executes in a container of its own that shares only the checkout with the agent's, reaching just the connections the Environment lists for it, never the agent's grants, model or tools.
- An Environment can also declare read-only caches, such as a package store, that every sandbox mounts and that only a trusted fill from the published main writes, so even pull request reviews install from warm caches.
- A setup network of its own, commands apart and read-only caches need container machines; microVM machines do not offer them.
- An agent's sandboxing is enforced by the server: a contained reviewer can run anything in its sandbox but changes nothing outside it and only reads through connections, a propose agent proposes but does not publish, and a publish agent may deploy and publish. Sandboxing is separate from the harness's own permission mode, which each agent also chooses.

### Code, models and sign-ins on the server

- Agents use Git in their sandboxes the ordinary way: fetches and pushes go through the gateway with a short-lived session grant, never the remote's credential. Pushes are limited to the project's work branches, and Work never updates the default branch of a repository it did not create.
- Automations can start a chat's checkout at any ref of the project's remote, such as a pull request's head, and move it when the pull request changes.
- Every chat on the server works on a branch of its own that starts from the repository's default branch. Work saves the branch, its commits and its uncommitted changes after each turn and gives them back when the workspace returns.
- The agent opens a pull request from its own commits with one tool, which also updates that pull request later and records it on the chat.
- Project agents can be Claude Code, Codex or an Agent Client Protocol agent such as OpenCode or Hermes on the server too. The agent runs in the chat's sandbox, on a worker or the server, and reaches its model through the gateway, which holds the organization's model key.
- The gateway can allow only the models the environment names, can pin which providers an aggregator such as OpenRouter routes to (with a few lines of the company's own code), and records usage per chat: tokens and the cost the provider reported, on OpenTelemetry spans and as totals for a chat and its subagents that projects build their own limits on.
- New sandbox model requests require the issuing turn attempt and its live lease; between-turn calls and old bearers on a later turn are denied. Git and HTTP background access keep their ordinary grant lifetime.
- Developers can instead use their own Claude subscription for Claude Code and their own ChatGPT subscription for Codex in their own remote chats. They sign in from the app on a machine of their own, in their own browser, with the harness's own login, and the sign-in stays on that machine: Work never copies or forwards it, model traffic goes straight to the provider, and a machine holds one person's sign-ins only. The machine has to persist, and whether that use is allowed under the provider's terms is the operator's to decide.
- Files such as `.env` that are never committed can reach a person's own chats too, in environments that allow it, on machines that isolate that person.

### Mobile and privacy

- The mobile companion (a PWA) pairs with the desktop by QR code over your LAN, or connects to your server, so a chat can continue from your phone.
- Incognito chats stay on the device and are never mirrored to a server, and a project can turn them off. They are separate from the browser's incognito tabs.
- A project's private working files are separate from shared project source.

## Install

- Mac with Apple silicon, macOS 13 or newer. Preview channel: `brew install --cask opencx-labs/tap/work@alpha`, or download the signed DMG from https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases.
- Downloads and release notes: https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases
